references.text: The Lord tells Abraham about the sin of Sodom and that He will investigate it – the background for the judgment on Lot's generation which Jesus refers to in [ref:Luk 17:28|Luke 17:28].

The account of Lot in Sodom, which Jesus points to. The inhabitants lived their daily lives – they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted, and built – until judgment struck them ([ref:1 Mos 19:1-15|Genesis 19:1-15]).
Fire and sulfur rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah and destroyed everything – the sudden judgment which Jesus uses as a pattern for the day of the Son of Man ([ref:1 Mos 19:24-25|Genesis 19:24-25]).

The preceding parallel with Noah's days: people ate, drank, married and were given in marriage until the flood came. Jesus uses the same pattern in [ref:Luk 17:26-27|Luke 17:26-27] as in the description of Lot's days.

The immediately following verse that completes the comparison: on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. So it will also be on the day the Son of Man is revealed ([ref:Luk 17:29-30|Luke 17:29-30]).

Jesus' parallel teaching in Matthew about Noah's days – people ate and drank and knew nothing until the flood came. The same point about unexpected judgment as in [ref:Matt 24:37-39|Matthew 24:37-39].
Isaiah describes people who eat, drink, and feast instead of repenting when judgment approaches – the same spiritual blindness that Jesus points to in [ref:Jes 22:12-13|Isaiah 22:12-13].

Ezekiel describes Sodom's sin as pride, abundance of food, and careless ease, without helping the poor and needy. This confirms the picture of a people occupied with daily tasks without thought of God's judgment ([ref:Esek 16:49-50|Ezekiel 16:49-50]).
Peter refers to Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of judgment on the ungodly, and that Lot was rescued – a New Testament parallel to Jesus' use of Lot's days ([ref:2 Pet 2:6-7|2 Peter 2:6-7]).

Paul writes that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When people say "peace and safety", then sudden destruction comes upon them – the same theme of unexpected judgment amid everyday security ([ref:1 Tess 5:2-3|1 Thessalonians 5:2-3]).
